title: I was in a 12-year relationship and it ended by email
text: Medium I was in a 12-year relationship and it ended by email | by Joel Caetano | Sep, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Medium Logo Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Doing the maths What was actually in there Why this one hurts differently The cold part The detail that gives me away Back to the joke Joel Caetano Gaming Videogames Personal Essay Product Management Software Engineering I was in a 12-year relationship and it ended by email Joel Caetano 6 min read · Just now -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size When I read the announcement, the first thing I felt wasn’t consumer disappointment. It was that thing in your stomach when someone says they need to talk to you. I’m talking about a video game. I know how that sounds. Give me three minutes. I started playing Destiny in 2014, the first one. I played the second. I played through job changes, house moves, entire phases of my life. Twelve years. And when they announced the end of support, my reaction was completely out of proportion to what had actually happened, a company decided to stop investing in a software product. That happens every day. It has happened to me dozens of times, with apps I used, services that shut down, tools that got deprecated. None of them left me like this. And it wasn’t really by email, it was a public announcement. But the feeling was the same, I found out through a text that wasn’t addressed to me. Doing the maths Twelve years. It’s worth looking at that number with some distance. Most of the friendships I had in 2014 no longer exist. I changed companies, changed routines, changed nearly everything. The group of people I speak to every week has turned over completely, family and a handful of others aside. And part of that handful, I met in there. If I said this about anything else, “I did this two or three times a week for twelve years, with the same people, and now it’s over”, nobody would find it strange that it got to me. A Saturday football group. A garage band. A running club. Nobody asks “but they were just training sessions, weren’t they?”. Because the place where it happened had graphics and a controller involved, the expected social response is a shrug. What was actually in there This is where the joke starts to stop being a joke. It isn’t the game I’m going to lose. It’s everything else. I should get one thing out of the way first. I was never good at it. Twelve years and I stayed bad. I didn’t improve with time, I never became the veteran who teaches the new guys, and I don’t have a single story where I show up and save the group. Which probably says something about why I kept going back. What I remember isn’t the numbers. It’s being stuck in the Vault of Glass jumping puzzle, me and another guy both convinced we knew “a foolproof shortcut”, launching ourselves into the abyss with total confidence and then hearing that sad little failed-jump sound followed by the awkward silence on comms. Forty minutes. Forty. I ended up sitting on a ledge waiting for everyone else to get across so I could join them, because otherwise we’d have been there all night. I remember Atheon. Teleported to Mars with two others, Relic in my hand, brain shutting down halfway through the Oracle spawns. I ran in circles screaming “WHAT’S THE BUTTON TO CLEANSE?!” while everyone else went blind from Mark of the Void because of me. I remember a PVP match on Shores of Time where I was getting humiliated as usual, dying at every corner, my K/D sinking faster than a rock on Venus. I came out of the tunnel, looked at the central platform, and instead of a wall of bullets I found a Warlock, alone, dancing. Completely relaxed. Having his own private cosmic disco in the middle of the Crucible. I stood there for two full seconds not processing it. Then I pulled out the sniper with all the time in the world, lined up the helmet in rhythm with his little dance steps, and pop. Headshot. Glorious ragdoll mid-choreography. I laughed alone into my mic like an idiot and saved the clip on the spot with the most honest title I’ve ever written: “Morreu a dançar”. He died dancing. It was 29 March 2015. I know the exact date because I still have the clip, eleven years later. I remember the loot cave, obviously. Hours shooting into a hole in a wall. I have no way of explaining that to anyone who wasn’t there. And mostly I remember being the one who caught every Taken blight explosion and got launched off the map, which, now that I think about it, is a decent summary of my entire career in that game. I could keep going. That’s the problem with pulling on this thread: every memory drags another one behind it, and at some point I realise I’m not writing an article, I’m taking inventory of twelve years. I’ll stop here, or this never ends. None of this is content. None of this shows up in a metric. This is twelve years of life shared with people I have, in most cases, never met in person. Why this one hurts differently Shows I loved have ended before. I’ve watched bands break up. It’s annoying, but it passes quickly, for one simple reason: the thing still exists. I can go back. The object is intact, waiting. A live service game isn’t an object. It’s a place. And that changes everything. When a place closes, it isn’t just the building that shuts. What closes is the possibility of going back there with those people, in that state, doing that thing. The café where your group met for years can still be standing under new ownership with new decor, and it still isn’t the place. Which is why “just play something else” solves nothing, in exactly the way “there are plenty more fish in the sea” has never solved anything for anyone. It wasn’t the game. It was that game, with those people, at that point in my life. The cold part Now the honest bit, otherwise this is just a grown man grieving a video game. From the outside, what happened was a perfectly rational business decision. Maintenance cost, active players, revenue
